newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW -- Maxwell sees $500 mln in revs.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -- Maxwell sees $500 mln in revs.

text.p: Ken Potashner, president and chief executive officer of Maxwell Laboritories Inc, is optimistic his company can produce $500 million in annual revenues within five to seven years.

The San Diego-based company, which started out as a niche player in the defense industry specializing in simulating nuclear explosions for the government, is aiming to turn its expertise into a variety of commercially lucrative applications as diverse as electrical car batteries to water purifiers.
"Maxwell aspires to be a billion dollar company," Potashner said in an interview Thursday.
Maxwell had $81 million in revenues in fiscal 1996.
"We will be a multi-hundred million dollar (revenue) company by the year 2000 and we're laying the framework to pursue becoming a billion dollar company," he said.
Potasher's outlook may be justified. When he joined the company on March 26, Maxwell's stock was slumbering at 6-7/8 and showing no indication of improvement.
The stock rose steadily and on October 18 reached the lofty height of 30 after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the company's "CoolPure" reduced temperature pazteurization process.
The product, made by its PurePulse Technologies unit, can eliminate E. coli, salmonella as well as other bacteria and viruses without altering the taste, smell or appearance of food products.
Last week an E. coli outbreak linked to Odwalla Inc juice products sent Maxwell's stock rising almost another 10 points, closing at 40 on Monday.
Revenues from the "CoolPure" product, a mere $5 million this year, will grow to more than $100 million in revenues within five year, Potashner predicted.

When Potashner came aboard, Maxwell relied on the government for about half of its revenues. He hopes to cut that to 25 percent by next year and plans to only sell products and services to the government that also have commercial applications.

The food purification product is just one of those that uses the company's core technology, which is called "Pulse Power." The technology, derived from the simulated nuclear explosions, allows the storage of large amounts of energy in small devices called Ultra Capacitors and then emits that energy at great speed.

Those Ultra Capacitors form the basis for what could be the most important segment of Maxwell's business, electrical batteries for mass-produced mainstream automobiles. The batteries will have longer-range and faster acceleration than older electrical cars batteries.
"The market potential for our product is in the $300 million range by the year 2002," Potashner said.
Maxwell has already signed an agreement and begun shipping batteries to "one of the major car companies."
Other areas of high potential high growth include the company's information technologies business which has signed a pact with Yahoo Inc on Internet traffic mapping.
